title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
directAnswer: Unlimited transactions (buy then sell, repeat) — the maximum profit is simply the sum of every positive day-to-day price increase: profit = Σ max(0, prices[i] − prices[i−1]). Capturing every upward step is provably optimal because any multi-day gain telescopes into consecutive deltas, and skipping the negative ones loses nothing. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Greedy — sum of positive consecutive deltas
rules: Add up **every positive delta** `prices[i] − prices[i−1]`; ignore non-positive ones.
This equals buying at every **valley** and selling at every **peak** — the two views are identical.
**Unlimited transactions** is the key permission; with a limit, greedy breaks and you need DP.
You may sell and rebuy the **same day**, so capturing each up-step independently is legal.
The greedy result is provably optimal because gains **telescope**: a long climb = sum of its daily steps.
whenToUse: Unlimited buy/sell transactions on a price (or value) series
Maximize total gain from any sequence of up-moves
Problems framed as 'capture all upward movement'
When holding one unit at a time and same-day re-entry is allowed
antiSignals: At most k (or 1, or 2) transactions → DP over (day, transactions, holding) — greedy fails
Cooldown or transaction fee → DP state machine (LC 309 / 714)
Must hold across the whole period → that's Stock I (single buy/sell, track min)
Short selling allowed → the 'only capture ups' argument no longer holds
remember.takeaway: When transactions are unlimited, the answer collapses to 'grab every up-step'. Internalize the telescoping proof — it turns a scary 'when to buy and sell' search into a one-line sum, and it cleanly contrasts with the DP needed once a transaction cap appears.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize that unlimited transactions makes the problem greedy, and whether you can PROVE summing positive deltas is optimal rather than just asserting it.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to find the single global min and max (Stock I thinking), or overcomplicating with a transaction-tracking DP when greedy suffices.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Prove the greedy via telescoping (a buy-low/sell-high spanning days equals the sum of the daily deltas in between), then mention the DP state machine as the framework that survives when a transaction limit is added.

problemStatement:
You are given an integer array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a given stock on the `i`-th day.

On each day, you may decide to buy and/or sell the stock. You can only hold **at most one** share of the stock at any time. However, you can buy it then immediately sell it on the **same day**.

Find and return the **maximum profit** you can achieve.
understanding: With unlimited transactions and at-most-one share held, you want the maximum total profit. The optimum is to capture every upward price movement: buy before each rise and sell at its top. Equivalently, sum all positive consecutive differences.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many transactions am I allowed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Unlimited. That's the whole difference from Stock I/III/IV — unlimited transactions is exactly what makes the greedy sum-of-positive-deltas optimal.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I hold more than one share?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, at most one share at a time. But I can sell and immediately rebuy on the same day, which is what lets me treat each up-step independently.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is there a transaction fee or cooldown?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. If there were, the pure greedy would break and I'd switch to a DP state machine (those are LC 714 and 309).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can prices be flat or strictly decreasing?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Flat or decreasing stretches contribute zero profit — we simply add nothing on non-positive deltas, never a loss.

examples.explanation: Buy at 1, sell at 5 (profit 4); buy at 3, sell at 6 (profit 3). Total 7 = positive deltas (5−1)+(6−3).
Every day rises. Sum of deltas 1+1+1+1 = 4, same as one buy at 1 / sell at 5.
Monotonically decreasing — no positive delta exists, so the best is to never trade.

diagrams.title: Greedy vs DP for stock problems
diagrams.caption: Unlimited transactions → greedy. A transaction cap or fee/cooldown → DP.

approaches.name: Greedy — Sum of Positive Deltas (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this and prove it. The proof (telescoping) is what separates a strong answer from 'I just summed the ups'.
hints: If the price goes up from one day to the next, could you always have profited from that single step by holding across it?
Any profit from buying on day i and selling on day j > i equals the sum of the consecutive daily changes between them. What does that let you ignore?
Add prices[i] - prices[i-1] whenever it's positive; skip it otherwise. The total is the maximum profit.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass comparing each adjacent pair → O(n) time. Only a running profit accumulator → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
With unlimited transactions and the ability to rebuy the same day, the problem stops being a search over (buy-day, sell-day) pairs and collapses into a one-line sum. Here is *why*.

**The telescoping identity.** Suppose the optimal plan buys on day `b` and sells on day `s` (`b < s`). Its profit is `prices[s] − prices[b]`. Now rewrite that single span as a sum of consecutive daily steps: `prices[s] − prices[b] = (prices[b+1] − prices[b]) + (prices[b+2] − prices[b+1]) + … + (prices[s] − prices[s−1])`. The intermediate terms cancel — it *telescopes*. So holding one share from day `b` to day `s` earns exactly the same as making a fresh buy-and-sell on every single day in between (legal, since same-day rebuy is allowed). The two strategies are **profit-equivalent**.

**Why dropping the negative steps is optimal.** Once any held span equals the sum of its daily deltas, we're free to decompose the whole timeline into daily decisions: for each day-to-day step we can choose to 'be holding' (earn that delta) or 'be flat' (earn 0). To maximize the total we obviously include a step exactly when its delta is positive and exclude it when it's negative or zero. There is no coupling between days — each step's contribution is independent — so the greedy choice per step is globally optimal. That independence is the crux: with unlimited transactions, a locally good choice can never hurt a future one.

**Why this fails the moment transactions are capped.** If you may make at most `k` trades, the steps are no longer independent — spending a transaction on a small up-move might cost you a bigger one later, so you must compare alternatives, which is what DP does. The greedy's correctness rests entirely on 'unlimited', and saying so out loud shows you understand the boundary of the technique.

**Geometric reading.** Plot the prices as a zig-zag. The greedy sum is the total vertical height of all the *rising* edges. Buying at every valley and selling at every peak captures exactly those rising edges and none of the falling ones — which is the same number the formula produces.
approaches.insight: Unlimited transactions + same-day rebuy makes each daily price step an independent yes/no decision worth max(0, delta). Telescoping proves a long hold never beats the sum of its steps, so 'grab every up-step' is optimal — no search needed.

approaches.name: DP State Machine — Hold vs Cash
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the framework that generalizes: it survives transaction fees, cooldowns, and caps where the greedy doesn't. Shows you know the broader stock-problem family.
hints: Track two running states each day: the best profit while holding a share, and the best profit while holding cash (no share).
Transitions: cash today = max(stay in cash, sell the share we held); hold today = max(keep holding, buy with our cash).
Because transactions are unlimited, buying simply spends the current cash balance — no transaction counter needed. Answer is the final cash state.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two O(1) state updates per day across one pass → O(n) time. Two scalars carried forward → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
The DP view models each day as a tiny state machine with two states — `cash` (no share held) and `hold` (one share held) — and asks for the best achievable profit in each.

**The two transitions.** On day `i` with price `p`:
- `cash = max(cash, hold + p)` — either we stay in cash, or we sell the share we were holding, adding `p` to whatever profit `hold` represented.
- `hold = max(hold, cashPrev − p)` — either we keep holding, or we buy today, spending `p` out of yesterday's cash.

The subtle correctness point is ordering: when updating `hold`, we want *yesterday's* cash, not the cash we may have just updated this same day. In the unlimited case it turns out updating `cash` first and then `hold` still yields the right answer (selling then rebuying the same day is allowed and is profit-neutral when `p` cancels), but the clean mental model is to compute both from the previous day's values.

**Why this reduces to the greedy here.** With unlimited transactions there's no transaction counter to track, so the state space stays at two scalars. Expanding the recurrence, `cash` ends up accumulating exactly the positive deltas — the DP and the greedy compute the *same number*. The DP just arrives at it through a more general lens.

**Why bother with the heavier method.** The DP framework is the one that *keeps working* when the problem grows teeth: add a per-transaction fee and the sell transition becomes `hold + p − fee`; add a cooldown and you introduce a third state; cap transactions at `k` and you add a dimension. The greedy can't bend that way. Presenting the DP signals you can solve the whole Stock I–IV / 309 / 714 family from one template, which is exactly what a follow-up will probe.
approaches.insight: Model trading as a two-state machine (cash/hold) and write the max-profit transitions. It collapses to the greedy when transactions are unlimited, but unlike the greedy it extends to fees, cooldowns, and transaction caps — making it the reusable backbone of every stock problem.

dryRun.intro: cash starts 0, hold starts -∞ (or -prices[0]). Each day update cash then hold from the running values.

code.python:
def maxProfit(self, prices: list[int]) -> int:
    cash = 0
    hold = float('-inf')
    for p in prices:
        prev_cash = cash
        cash = max(cash, hold + p)
        hold = max(hold, prev_cash - p)
    return cash

Best profit while holding a share; impossible before any buy → -∞.
Stay in cash, or sell today's share for p.
Keep holding, or buy today using yesterday's cash.

python.explanation: Profit with no share — the eventual answer.
Holding a share is impossible until the first buy.
Sell transition adds p to the holding profit.
Buy transition spends prior cash on a share.

edgeCases.behavior: One day: hold = -2, cash stays 0 → return 0.

pitfalls: Updating hold from the just-updated cash instead of prevCash — muddles the model (harmless here, wrong once a fee/cooldown is added).
Initializing hold to 0 instead of -∞ — pretends you own a free share.
Adding a transaction counter you don't need — transactions are unlimited.

commonMistakes: Solving it like Stock I (single global min-to-max) and undercounting multi-swing profit.
Believing you can't rebuy the same day — you can, which legitimizes capturing each up-step.
Reaching for a transaction-counting DP when unlimited transactions make greedy sufficient.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Treating it as a single buy/sell (Stock I)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Finding one min and one later max ignores that you can re-enter. On [1,2,1,2] the single-trade answer is 1, but capturing both up-steps gives 2.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
min_price, best = prices[0], 0
for p in prices:
    min_price = min(min_price, p)
    best = max(best, p - min_price)
return best

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Buying at a valley but waiting for the global peak
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Holding through a dip forfeits the smaller swings. You must sell at every local peak and rebuy at every local valley — equivalently, add every positive delta.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Initializing the DP hold state to 0
commonMistakesDetailed.why: hold = 0 implies you start already owning a share for free, inflating profit. It must be -∞ (or -prices[0] after the first day) so the first buy is paid for.

patternNote: Greedy capture of positive deltas for unlimited-transaction profit, with the cash/hold DP as the generalizable backbone. Recognise the greedy whenever local choices are independent; switch to the DP state machine the moment a transaction cap, fee, or cooldown couples the decisions.
